channel.title: TalkLive Blog
channel.description: Guides and research on talking to strangers, voice chat, language practice and online safety - from the team behind TalkLive.

item.title: How Many Hours Does It Take to Make a Friend?
item.description: About 50 hours together turns an acquaintance into a casual friend, about 90 into a friend and more than 200 into a close friend, according to research by Jeffrey Hall. What counts, what does not, and how adults can make friends faster.

item.title: 怎样免费练英语口语：和外国陌生人说话的实用指南
item.description: 背了很多单词却开不了口？研究表明，开口说才是练口语的关键。本文介绍每天10分钟的练习方法、开场白和救场句、和各国人聊天的最佳时间，以及在线和陌生人聊天时如何保护自己。

item.title: The Compliment You Didn’t Give
item.description: You notice something good about someone and say nothing, because it might be awkward. Experiments on compliments and thank-you letters show we badly underestimate how much they land, and why that keeps us quiet.

item.title: Nobody Noticed: The Spotlight Effect
item.description: You stumble over a word on a call and feel it echo for an hour. Classic experiments show other people notice our slips, nerves and accents far less than we think, and knowing that can make you calmer.

item.title: Why We Laugh in Conversation (It Is Rarely the Jokes)
item.description: Most laughter does not follow anything funny. Studies of real conversations show we laugh to connect, that speakers laugh more than listeners, and that people across the world can hear friendship in a laugh.

item.title: Why Boredom Hurts So Much, and What It Is Trying to Tell You
item.description: In one experiment, people chose to give themselves electric shocks rather than sit alone with their thoughts for fifteen minutes. What boredom really is, why scrolling rarely fixes it, and what does.

item.title: How to End a Conversation Without Being Rude
item.description: Almost no conversation ends when both people want it to. What a Harvard study found about conversations that run too long or too short, how linguists describe a good goodbye, and exact words to use, in person, on a call or with a stranger online.

item.title: The Introvert's Guide to Talking to Strangers
item.description: Introverts enjoy talking to strangers more than they predict, and pay for it later. What the research on acting extraverted actually shows, how to budget your social battery, and a gentle way to start.

item.title: Small Talk Around the World: What to Say, and What Not to Ask
item.description: Why "Have you eaten?" means hello in China, why Finns are fine with silence, and why Koreans ask your age. A passport of greetings, safe openers and questions to save for later in 12 countries.

item.title: Why One Phone Call Beats Fifty Texts
item.description: People pick texting because they expect calls to be awkward. Experiments say they are wrong: a voice builds more connection, carries tone that text loses, and even changes stress hormones. What the research shows, and the myth it replaces.

item.title: New City, No One to Call: Loneliness After Moving Abroad
item.description: Around 280 million people live outside the country they were born in, and loneliness is one of the most common things they share. The real shape of culture shock, the two kinds of loneliness, and a practical plan for the first months.

item.title: Why It Is Sometimes Easier to Tell a Stranger the Truth
item.description: People confess things to strangers on trains that they never tell their friends. A sociologist noticed this in 1908. Here is what is going on, and where it stops working.

item.title: The Rise and Fall of Omegle: Fourteen Years of Talking to Strangers
item.description: An 18-year-old built Omegle in his bedroom in 2009. It closed in November 2023 with a note about cost, misuse and a heart attack in his thirties. How it got there, and what it left behind.

item.title: We Are Bad at Predicting How Talking to Strangers Will Feel
item.description: Commuters, coffee queues and first conversations: a decade of experiments shows people consistently underestimate how much they will enjoy talking to strangers. Six studies, and their limits.

item.title: Loneliness Is Not the Same as Being Alone
item.description: You can be lonely in a full house and content on your own. What loneliness really is, why it makes people pull away, and the surprising finding about which kinds of help work best.

item.title: What Actually Happens in the Two Seconds After You Press "Start"
item.description: A plain-English tour of a random voice match: the waiting queue, why filters make you wait, the handshake that connects two browsers, and the relay that carries the audio when a direct line is impossible.

item.title: Listening Is a Skill. Most of Us Were Never Taught It.
item.description: Why we interrupt, the "shift response" that quietly steals conversations, and what research says about the single habit that makes people like you more. Ten questions about listening.

item.title: "Why Does My Heart Race Every Time the Phone Rings?"
item.description: A reader cannot make or answer phone calls without dread. Our reply on why calls are genuinely harder than texting, the habit that keeps the fear alive, and a step-by-step ladder out of it.

item.title: Why You Understand More Than You Can Say
item.description: Most learners can follow far more than they can say. A linguist called this out in 1985. Field notes on why speaking is its own skill, the fear that blocks it, and a four-week routine.

item.title: A Field Guide to the Scams That Start With "Hi"
item.description: Romance-to-crypto schemes, image blackmail, the "send me the code" trick and the bots that never answer a question. Seven common specimens, how to recognise each, and the one rule that defeats nearly all of them.

item.title: 30 Questions That Get Past Small Talk
item.description: In 1997 a psychologist made strangers feel close in 45 minutes with a list of questions that slowly got deeper. The idea behind it, why "what do you do?" stalls, and thirty questions in three tiers.
